title: Comparative Outcomes of the Next-Generation Extended Depth-of-Focus Intraocular Lens and Enhanced Monofocal Intraocular Lens in Cataract Surgery
condition_or_topic: Visual outcomes and spectacle dependence after cataract surgery with presbyopia-correcting intraocular lenses
clinical_background: Monofocal intraocular lenses provide good vision at a single focal distance but often leave patients needing spectacles for other activities. Multifocal intraocular lenses can improve intermediate and near vision, although light dispersion may reduce contrast sensitivity and increase photic phenomena. Extended depth-of-focus intraocular lenses aim to broaden the usable range of vision while limiting these disturbances. TECNIS PureSee™ uses a purely refractive design with a continuous change in power. Earlier preclinical and randomized studies reported improved intermediate and near vision relative to monofocal lenses, but its visual performance and patient satisfaction in routine clinical practice remained largely unknown.
objectives: Evaluate visual outcomes after implantation of TECNIS PureSee™ in a real-world cataract surgery setting, including distance, intermediate, and near visual acuity, defocus curves, and contrast sensitivity, compared with TECNIS Eyhance™.
Assess patient-reported photic phenomena, spectacle dependence, and satisfaction after implantation of the two lenses.
clinical_question: In patients undergoing bilateral cataract surgery, how does implantation of the PureSee™ EDOF (ZEN00V) intraocular lens compare with the Eyhance™ (ICB00) enhanced monofocal intraocular lens for postoperative visual acuity at different distances, defocus curves, contrast sensitivity, photic phenomena, spectacle dependence, and patient satisfaction?
interpretation: Compared with TECNIS Eyhance™ ICB00, TECNIS Puresee™ ZEN00V provided significantly better intermediate and near visual acuity, while distance acuity and contrast sensitivity remained comparable. Its binocular defocus curve generally favored ZEN00V, although the overall difference was not statistically significant. Near-vision spectacle dependence was lower with ZEN00V; intermediate-vision spectacle dependence was comparable. Photic phenomena occurred more often with ZEN00V, but the reported between-group differences were not statistically significant. The authors note that the more myopic postoperative SE in the ZEN00V group, despite a nonsignificant difference between groups, may have contributed to its intermediate and near outcomes. They also suggest that comparable distance acuity despite this residual refraction may indicate some tolerance of postoperative refractive error.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The authors describe their findings as consistent with a previous randomized clinical trial and optical-bench work on the refractive EDOF IOL. In the cited trial, intermediate acuity was 0.13 ± 0.08 with the refractive EDOF IOL versus 0.18 ± 0.14 with the enhanced monofocal IOL (p = 0.0127), and near acuity was 0.37 ± 0.10 logMAR versus 0.43 ± 0.16 (p = 0.0137); monocular CDVA was comparable. Earlier reports placed enhanced-monofocal monocular intermediate acuity at 0.16 to 0.30 logMAR and near acuity at 0.32 to 0.46 logMAR. Prior optical simulations suggested a range of vision comparable to diffractive EDF IOLs and greater tolerance of refractive error, while a previous trial also found a broader defocus range than with the enhanced monofocal IOL. Black et al. reported preservation of high-quality distance vision despite residual refractive error. In a separate retrospective study, Alfonso-Bartolozzi et al. reported three-month monocular UDVA of 0.10 ± 0.15 and corrected distance acuity of 0.05 ± 0.09 logMAR, with acuity below 0.20 logMAR from 0.00 D to −2.00 D on the monocular defocus curve. The authors also relate their contrast-sensitivity findings to earlier clinical reports of no mesopic compromise. They contrast the more frequent photic symptoms in their ZEN00V group with prior simulation findings of a monofocal-like profile and a clinical report in which most patients had no or minimal bother from halos (91.7%), stardusts (95.0%), and glare (95.0%).
clinical_implications: The refractive EDOF IOL may extend useful intermediate and near vision without a definite sacrifice in distance acuity or contrast sensitivity relative to the enhanced monofocal IOL.

The authors suggest that tolerance of some residual postoperative refractive error could support patient satisfaction, while acknowledging that predicting such error and pseudo-accommodation remains challenging.
Improved near-vision spectacle independence is a potential benefit, but photic phenomena were reported more frequently with ZEN00V.
practice_implications: The authors present TECNIS Puresee™ IOL as a potentially valuable option for cataract surgeons seeking distance and intermediate vision with functional near vision and acceptable photic phenomena.
They suggest that an EDOF IOL may be an option when tolerance of residual refractive error and an extended range of vision are desired.
limitations: The study was conducted at a single center, had a small sample, and included only Korean patients.
Its retrospective design imposes inherent limitations.
Visual quality was assessed subjectively through a questionnaire rather than with objective indicators such as optical aberrations.
Reading speed and stereopsis were not sufficiently assessed.
strengths: The authors note that binocular defocus curves enabled a comparison of refractive-error tolerance between the groups.
They state that their real-world clinical findings reproduced results from earlier simulations and a randomized clinical trial.
open_questions: How well the findings apply to larger or multicenter populations remains to be established.
Objective visual-quality outcomes, reading speed, and stereopsis after implantation of the new refractive EDOF IOL remain insufficiently evaluated.
future_directions: Validate the findings in larger studies or studies involving multiple centers.
Include objective measures of visual quality, such as optical aberrations, in future investigations.
Assess postoperative reading speed and stereopsis in recipients of the new refractive EDOF IOL.
study_design: Single-center retrospective comparison of patients who underwent bilateral cataract surgery between June 2021 and May 2024. The groups were matched 1:1 by age (±5 years).

population.description: The matched analysis included 100 eyes from 50 patients who received the same study lens in both eyes; each lens group comprised 25 patients and 50 eyes.
exclusion_criteria: Ocular abnormalities or diseases other than cataract that could affect postoperative visual acuity.
population.mean_age: 69.48 ± 5.83 years in the ZEN00V group; 72.44 ± 5.80 years in the ICB00 group
population.care_setting: Severance Eye Hospital, Seoul, South Korea; all procedures were performed by one surgeon.

interventions: Bilateral cataract surgery with conventional phacoemulsification and capsular-bag implantation of the TECNIS PureSee™ EDOF IOL (Model ZEN00V).
comparators: Bilateral cataract surgery with conventional phacoemulsification and capsular-bag implantation of the TECNIS Eyhance™ enhanced monofocal IOL (Model ICB00).

primary: Monocular uncorrected intermediate visual acuity (UIVA) at 66 cm and uncorrected near visual acuity (UNVA) at 40 cm were used for sample-size planning; the article does not explicitly designate primary outcomes.
secondary: Monocular uncorrected distance visual acuity (UDVA) and corrected distance visual acuity (CDVA).
Binocular defocus curves measured with the ETDRS chart at 4 m.
Contrast sensitivity at 1.5, 3, 6, 12, and 18 cycles per degree under photopic and mesopic conditions.
Questionnaire responses on halos, glare, starbursts, spectacle dependence by viewing distance, overall satisfaction, and willingness to recommend the implanted IOL.
Postoperative manifest refraction and spherical equivalent.

statistical_methods: Sample-size planning required 42 subjects for 80% power to detect a difference of 0.10 logMAR or greater in mean UIVA or UNVA, assuming a standard deviation of 0.16 logMAR and a two-sample t-test with a one-sided alpha of 0.025. Continuous baseline variables were summarized as mean ± standard deviation and categorical variables as counts and percentages. Categorical comparisons used Pearson’s chi-square test, or Fisher’s exact test when an expected cell frequency was less than 5; continuous comparisons used Student’s independent t-test. A generalized estimating equation (GEE) with an exchangeable correlation structure accounted for correlation between eyes in monocular comparisons. Missing data were not imputed. Analyses were otherwise two-tailed, with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant, using SPSS version 22.0 and R version 4.3.3.
follow_up: Patients were assessed one day, one week, one month, and three months after surgery, with postoperative outcomes evaluated at three months. A separate measurement description states that distance visual acuity was measured at 4 months.

secondary_results: Before matching, 58 eyes from 29 patients in the ZEN00V group and 68 eyes from 34 patients in the ICB00 group were evaluated; there were no missing medical records or losses to follow-up before the 3-month assessment. The matched analysis included 100 eyes from 50 patients: ZEN00V, 25 patients/50 eyes; ICB00, 25 patients/50 eyes. All analyzed participants completed three months of follow-up.

Baseline age was 69.48 ± 5.83 years with ZEN00V and 72.44 ± 5.80 years with ICB00 (p = 0.30). The ZEN00V group included 5 (20%) male and 20 (80%) female patients; the ICB00 group included 9 (36%) male and 16 (64%) female patients (sex comparison p = 0.06).
Baseline UDVA was 0.38 ± 0.29 logMAR with ZEN00V and 0.48 ± 0.34 logMAR with ICB00 (p = 0.20). Baseline BCVA was 0.15 ± 0.19 logMAR and 0.23 ± 0.27 logMAR, respectively (p = 0.13).

Baseline spherical equivalent was 0.88 ± 1.62 D with ZEN00V and 0.65 ± 1.63 D with ICB00 (p = 0.68). K1 was 43.66 ± 1.11 D and 43.63 ± 1.63 D, respectively (p = 0.93); K2 was 44.21 ± 1.11 D and 44.33 ± 1.55 D (p = 0.75). Axis was 86.94 ± 46.09◦ and 96.54 ± 60.44◦ (p = 0.42), and axial length was 23.54 ± 0.66 mm and 23.61 ± 0.83 mm (p = 0.74).

The cited earlier randomized clinical study reported intermediate visual acuity of 0.13 ± 0.08 with the refractive EDOF IOL and 0.18 ± 0.14 with the enhanced monofocal IOL, with an improvement of 0.05 logMAR (p = 0.0127). Its near visual acuity results were 0.37 ± 0.10 logMAR and 0.43 ± 0.16 logMAR, respectively (p = 0.0137); monocular CDVA was comparable.
Other cited studies of the enhanced monofocal IOL reported monocular intermediate visual acuity ranging from 0.16 to 0.30 logMAR and near visual acuity ranging from 0.32 to 0.46 logMAR.

A cited retrospective study by Alfonso-Bartolozzi et al. reported postoperative monocular UDVA of 0.10 ± 0.15 logMAR and corrected distance visual acuity of 0.05 ± 0.09 logMAR at three months. Its monocular defocus curve remained below 0.20 logMAR from 0.00 D to −2.00 D.
The cited prior clinical study reported that most patients experienced no or minimal disturbance from halos (91.7%), stardusts (95.0%) and glare (95.0%).

The discussion reports 100% spectacle independence with the new refractive EDOF IOL in a cited prior study. It also states that other studies of the enhanced monofocal IOL reported 100% independence from intermediate-vision spectacles and moderate independence from near-vision spectacles.

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that TECNIS Puresee™ improved intermediate and near vision relative to the enhanced monofocal IOL without a significant reduction in distance acuity or contrast sensitivity. They consider it a promising cataract-surgery option for presbyopia correction, with greater near-spectacle independence and acceptable photic phenomena.
narrative_summary: This single-center retrospective study compared bilateral cataract surgery with the refractive EDOF TECNIS PureSee™ ZEN00V and the enhanced monofocal TECNIS Eyhance™ ICB00. Age-matched analyses included 100 eyes from 50 patients, with outcomes assessed three months after surgery. Monocular intermediate acuity at 66 cm favored ZEN00V: 0.11 ± 0.08 versus 0.17 ± 0.11 logMAR (p = 0.006). Near acuity at 40 cm also favored ZEN00V: 0.25 ± 0.07 versus 0.31 ± 0.13 logMAR (p = 0.023). Uncorrected distance acuity was comparable at 0.08 ± 0.10 versus 0.10 ± 0.11 logMAR (p = 0.53). Contrast sensitivity did not differ significantly across the measured spatial frequencies under photopic or mesopic conditions without glare. The ZEN00V defocus curve showed significantly better vision at −1.0 D and from −2.50 D to −3.50 D. Near-spectacle dependence was 9 (36%) with ZEN00V versus 20 (80%) with ICB00 (p = 0.002); photic phenomena occurred more often with ZEN00V, although the listed comparisons were not statistically significant. The authors regard the extended range of vision as clinically promising. They caution that the retrospective study was small, conducted at one center, and confined to Koreans; vision-quality assessment relied on a subjective questionnaire, while reading speed and stereopsis were not sufficiently evaluated.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: The study evaluated real-world outcomes after bilateral cataract surgery with the purely refractive PureSee™ EDOF (ZEN00V), which uses a continuous power change, against the enhanced monofocal Eyhance™ (ICB00). This single-institution retrospective analysis included 100 eyes from 50 patients. Visual acuity, defocus curves, contrast sensitivity and patient-reported outcomes were evaluated three months after surgery. Compared with ICB00, ZEN00V produced better uncorrected intermediate acuity (0.11 ± 0.08 vs. 0.17 ± 0.11 logMAR, p = 0.006) and near acuity (0.25 ± 0.08 vs. 0.31 ± 0.13 logMAR, p = 0.023), with similar distance acuity. The groups had comparable defocus curves and contrast sensitivity overall. Photic phenomena occurred more often with ZEN00V, whereas near-spectacle dependence was lower (36% vs. 80%, p = 0.002); dependence at intermediate and far distances was comparable. The authors considered PureSee™ a promising presbyopia-correction option because it improved intermediate and near vision while largely preserving distance vision, contrast sensitivity and patient satisfaction.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: Advances in preoperative biometry, IOL power calculations, surgery and lens technology have improved cataract-surgery outcomes. Monofocal IOLs are commonly used because they provide strong vision at one focal distance, relatively few photic phenomena and relatively low cost. Their fixed focal distance nevertheless leaves many patients needing spectacles for daily activities. Presbyopia-correcting lenses seek to reduce that dependence. Multifocal IOLs can improve intermediate and near vision, but their refractive and diffractive designs disperse some light, potentially lowering contrast sensitivity and increasing photic disturbances and dissatisfaction. Residual refractive error is an important cause of poorer postoperative vision with multifocal IOLs. Their use remains constrained when power prediction is difficult, including in short eyes, highly myopic eyes and eyes previously treated with refractive surgery. EDOF IOLs seek a more continuous range of vision between intermediate and far distances while limiting unwanted photic effects; prior reports describe modest intermediate-vision gains and photic phenomena similar to conventional monofocal lenses. TECNIS PureSee™ has a purely refractive design with a continuously varying power profile intended to preserve visual quality and contrast sensitivity. Earlier preclinical and randomized clinical studies reported better intermediate and near vision than monofocal IOLs, with comparable distance vision and photic phenomena. Its performance and patient satisfaction in routine clinical practice remained largely uncertain. This study therefore compared postoperative distance, intermediate and near vision, contrast sensitivity and defocus curves after TECNIS PureSee™ implantation with outcomes after Eyhance™ implantation, an enhanced monofocal lens that also slightly extends depth of focus.

document_sections.heading: 2.1. Study Design and Participants
document_sections.content: The investigators retrospectively examined clinical records from patients who underwent cataract surgery at Severance Eye Hospital, Yonsei University College of medicine, Seoul, Korea, between June 2021 and May 2024. Eligible patients were over 40 years old and had preoperative astigmatism ≤ 1.0 diopter (D). Exclusion criteria were age over 85 years, axial length > 26.0 mm or <22.5 mm, previous ocular surgery or trauma, ocular abnormalities or non-cataract disease capable of affecting postoperative acuity, and intra- or post-operative complications. The axial-length exclusion above >26.0 mm was based on earlier reports linking elongated eyes with absolute prediction error. Cases were matched one-to-one (1:1), with control eyes matched for age within ±5 years.

document_sections.heading: 2.2. Surgical Technique
document_sections.content: Tae-Im Kim performed every operation at Severance Eye Hospital in Seoul, South Korea. Surgery used topical 0.5% proparacaine hydrochloride. The main incision followed the steepest corneal axis, and a 20 G paracentesis was created. Conventional phacoemulsification, irrigation, aspiration and capsule polishing used the Centurion Vision System. The IOL was placed in the capsular bag, and stromal hydration sealed the incisions.

document_sections.heading: 2.3. IOLs
document_sections.content: The study compared the TECNIS PureSee™ EDOF IOL (Model ZEN00V) with the TECNIS Eyhance™ enhanced monofocal IOL (Model ICB00). ZEN00V is a one-piece, foldable, soft-acrylic, aspheric posterior-chamber refractive EDOF lens. Its total diameter is 13.0 mm and its optic diameter is 6.0 mm. Its biconvex, wavefront-designed aspheric anterior surface compensates for average corneal spherical aberration; a continuously varying power on its refractive posterior surface extends depth of focus. ICB00 is a one-piece, foldable, hydrophobic soft-acrylic posterior-chamber lens with the same overall geometry and dimensions. Its higher-order aspheric anterior surface changes power continuously from periphery to center to extend depth of focus slightly. Both lenses have an optical A-constant of 119.3 and powers from +5.0 D to +34.0 D in 0.5 D increments.

document_sections.heading: 2.4. Measurements
document_sections.content: Before surgery, participants underwent screening for ocular and systemic disease, acuity and manifest-refraction assessments, intraocular-pressure measurement, keratometry, slit-lamp and dilated-fundus examinations, specular microscopy and optical biometry. Acuity testing used photopic illumination of 85 candelas/square meter (cd/m2) and 100% contrast. Monocular CDVA and UDVA were measured at 4 months with an ETDRS chart; monocular UIVA at 66 cm and UNVA at 40 cm used handheld ETDRS cards. Acuities were converted to logMAR for analysis. Manifest refraction followed standard optometric methods. The Topcon KR 8800 measured keratometry, the IOL Master 700 provided optical biometry, and the EM-4000 provided specular microscopy. Implanted-lens power was calculated with the Barrett Universal II formula without individualized IOL-constant adjustment. Lens power targeted a slightly myopic postoperative refraction of −0.25D.

document_sections.heading: 2.5. Postoperative Outcome Measures
document_sections.content: Patients were examined one day, one week, one month and three months after cataract surgery. At three months, monocular CDVA and UDVA were assessed as before surgery, while handheld ETDRS cards measured monocular UIVA at 66 cm and UNVA at 40 cm. For binocular defocus curves, investigators began at +1.50 D spherical relative to manifest refraction and added negative spherical trial lenses in −0.50 D increments through −4.00 D. The BCVA trial frame was retained to limit vertex-distance effects; an ETDRS chart at 4 m measured binocular acuity at each step. Contrast sensitivity with subjective refraction was assessed without glare under photopic target luminance of 85 cd/m2 and mesopic target luminance of 3 cd/m2, at 1.5, 3, 6, 12 and 18 cycles per degree. The F.A.C.T used the Optec 6500 system under controlled photopic and mesopic lighting. A postoperative questionnaire asked about halo, glare and starburst, spectacle use for distance, intermediate and near tasks, overall satisfaction, and willingness to recommend the same IOL. Answers were recorded as ‘yes’ or ‘no’; the questionnaire is supplied as Table S1.

document_sections.heading: 2.6. Statistical Analysis
document_sections.content: The sample-size calculation required 42 subjects for 80% power to detect a between-group mean-acuity difference of 0.10 logMAR or greater in UIVA and UNVA. It assumed a standard deviation of 0.16 logMAR and a two-sample t-test with one-sided alpha of 0.025; each study group contained more than 42 eyes. Continuous baseline variables were summarized as mean ± standard deviation, and categorical variables as counts and percentages. Missing observations were not imputed. Categorical comparisons used Pearson’s chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test when any expected cell frequency was less than 5; continuous comparisons used Student’s independent t-test. A generalized estimating equation (GEE) with exchangeable correlation accounted for correlation between eyes in monocular group comparisons. Tests were two-tailed, with p-value < 0.05 defining statistical significance. Analyses used SPSS version 22.0 and R version 4.3.3.

document_sections.heading: 3. Results
document_sections.content: Initially evaluated were 58 eyes from 29 patients in the ZEN00V group and 68 eyes from 34 patients in the ICB00 group. There were no missing medical records or losses to follow-up before the 3-month assessment. Four ZEN00V patients and six ICB00 patients were excluded because of intra- or post-operative complications. The matched analysis comprised 100 eyes from 50 patients: ZEN00V IOL (n = 50) and ICB00 IOL (n = 50), implanted bilaterally. Table 1 presents preoperative characteristics. Mean age was 69.48 ± 5.83 years with ZEN00V and 72.44 ± 5.80 years with ICB00 (p = 0.30). Preoperative SE was 0.88 ± 1.62 and 0.65 ± 1.63, respectively (p = 0.68). Women predominated in both groups (p = 0.06). Preoperative uncorrected acuity was 0.38 ± 0.29 vs. 0.48 ± 0.34 (p = 0.20), and best-corrected acuity was 0.15 ± 0.19 vs. 0.23 ± 0.27 (p = 0.13); these baseline measures were comparable. No included participant was reported to have endophthalmitis, secondary glaucoma, cystoid macular edema or another intra- or post-operative complication. All included participants completed three months of follow-up. Table 2 summarizes three-month refraction and visual acuity. Postoperative SE was −0.46 ± 0.60D with ZEN00V and −0.28 ± 0.27 D with ICB00 (p = 0.09). UDVA was 0.08 ± 0.10 vs. 0.10 ± 0.11 (p = 0.53), and CDVA was 0.01 ± 0.03 vs. 0.01 ± 0.02 (p = 0.21), without significant between-group differences. At 66 cm, monocular UIVA favored ZEN00V: 0.11 ± 0.08 logMAR vs. 0.17 ± 0.11 logMAR (p = 0.006). At 40 cm, mean UNVA likewise favored ZEN00V: 0.25 ± 0.07 logMAR vs. 0.31 ± 0.13 logMAR (p = 0.023). Monocular UIVA better than 0.20 logMAR was attained by 72% (36/50) of ZEN00V eyes and 50% (25/50) of ICB00 eyes; UNVA better than 0.20 logMAR was attained by 14% (7/50) and 10% (5/50), respectively. Figure 1 presents binocular defocus curves. Both had a U-shaped profile with best acuity at 0.00 D. ZEN00V generally performed better except at +1.5 D, although the general difference was not statistically significant. Direct comparisons showed significantly better defocused vision with ZEN00V at −1.0 D and from −2.50 D to −3.50 D. Its mean binocular acuity remained better than 0.20 logMAR from +1.00 D to –1.50 D. Figure 2 presents contrast sensitivity without glare: no spatial frequency showed a significant group difference under photopic or mesopic conditions (all p > 0.05). Table 3 presents questionnaire findings. With ZEN00V, four patients (16%) reported halos, four (16%) glare and one (4%) starbursts; with ICB00, two patients (8%) reported halos and no other photic symptom was noted (all p > 0.05). Neither group reported a need for distance spectacles (p > 0.05). One patient per group needed intermediate correction (p > 0.05). For near correction, the results narrative reports 20 patients (20%) with ICB00 and 9 (36%) with ZEN00V (p = 0.002); Table 3 instead gives 20 (80%) for ICB00. Satisfaction exceeded 90% in both groups, and 100% of each group said they would recommend its IOL type.

document_sections.heading: 4. Discussion
document_sections.content: The authors interpret their comparison of TECNIS Puresee™ ZEN00V and TECNIS Eyhance™ ICB00 as showing a wider range of vision with the refractive EDOF lens while maintaining comparable distance acuity. Intermediate and near acuity were significantly better with ZEN00V; its binocular defocus performance was generally better, while mesopic and photopic contrast sensitivity remained comparable at all tested spatial frequencies. A previously published multicenter, double-blind RCT and optical-bench work supported these findings. The previous clinical study found similar monocular CDVA between lenses; intermediate acuity was 0.13 ± 0.08 with the refractive EDOF IOL and 0.18 ± 0.14 with the enhanced monofocal IOL, a difference of 0.05 logMAR (p = 0.0127). Its near-acuity values were 0.37 ± 0.10 logMAR and 0.43 ± 0.16, respectively (p = 0.0137). Other studies of enhanced monofocal IOLs reported monocular intermediate acuity from 0.16 to 0.30 logMAR and near acuity from 0.32 to 0.46 logMAR; the authors regard those results as broadly consistent with both the RCT and their study. They also note that ZEN00V eyes had a more myopic postoperative SE, without a statistically significant group difference, which may have contributed to their superior intermediate and near acuity. Both study lenses had single-focus defocus profiles extending into intermediate vision, with peak acuity at 0.00 D. ZEN00V showed a generally better curve, including <0.10 logMAR from +0.50 D to −1.00 D and <0.20 logMAR from +1.00 D to −1.50 D. Earlier optical-bench simulations suggested a vision range comparable to diffractive EDF IOLs and greater refractive-error tolerance. An earlier RCT measured monocular distance-corrected defocus from +1.00 D to −2.50 D and found a wider range with the refractive EDOF lens than with the enhanced monofocal lens. A follow-up report by Black et al. described monofocal-comparable distance quality with the refractive EDOF lens despite residual refractive error. The authors note that postoperative refractive error and pseudo-accommodation remain difficult to predict completely; residual error can particularly impair multifocal-IOL performance. They suggest an EDOF lens may offer extended vision and greater residual-error tolerance without a definite acuity disadvantage relative to monofocal IOLs. In a separate single-center retrospective study, Alfonso-Bartolozzi et al. reported three-month monocular UDVA of 0.10 ± 0.15 logMAR and corrected distance acuity of 0.05 ± 0.09 logMAR after implantation of the new refractive EDOF IOL. That study found monocular acuity below 0.20 logMAR from 0.00 D to −2.00 D on defocus testing; the authors consider its visual findings broadly consistent with theirs. Contrast-sensitivity testing can capture aspects of object identification and spatial visual quality beyond acuity. Earlier work has associated multifocal and EDOF IOLs with possible contrast-sensitivity reductions. Multifocal lenses form simultaneous retinal images at different distances, potentially introducing overlapping blurred images; EDOF designs instead provide a continuous focus range that may limit secondary out-of-focus images. TECNIS Puresee™ was designed to reduce photic disturbances: its gradually changing posterior curvature produces a continuous refractive-power change intended to eliminate scatter sources. In the present study, glare-free contrast sensitivity did not differ between groups under mesopic or photopic illumination across spatial frequencies. Previous clinical reports likewise described preserved mesopic contrast sensitivity and high-quality distance vision. Fewer than 20% of ZEN00V patients reported photic phenomena on the study questionnaire, although these phenomena were more frequent than with ICB00 at three months. Earlier optical-bench and simulation studies reported a dysphotopsia profile similar to monofocal IOLs in the presence of refractive error. In a previous clinical study, most patients reported either no symptoms or minimal bother from halos (91.7%), stardusts (95.0%) and glare (95.0%). The authors suggest that the refractive lens’s smooth posterior-curvature change may help explain its monofocal-like dysphotopsia profile, while acknowledging the greater frequency observed in their ZEN00V group. The discussion describes greater intermediate- and near-spectacle independence with the refractive EDOF lens, consistent with the authors’ acuity and defocus interpretation; the study’s questionnaire results report the same intermediate-correction need in both groups. A prior study reported 100% spectacle independence with the refractive EDOF lens, while other enhanced-monofocal studies reported 100% independence at intermediate distance and moderate independence for near vision. The authors expect demand for spectacle-free intermediate and near vision to grow with longevity and attention to quality of life; they cite an anticipated presbyopia burden of approximately 2.1 billion by 2030. They expect the refractive EDOF lens to broaden vision while retaining monofocal-comparable distance acuity. In their data, UDVA was comparable despite more myopic mean postoperative SE with ZEN00V, suggesting some tolerance of residual refractive error that may improve satisfaction. The authors identify a single Korean center, small sample and retrospective design as limitations, and call for larger or multicenter studies. Visual quality was assessed subjectively by questionnaire; future studies using objective measures such as optical aberrations could broaden its evaluation. They note that binocular defocus curves did allow comparison of refractive-error tolerance. Reading speed and stereopsis were insufficiently assessed and warrant postoperative investigation.

document_sections.heading: 5. Conclusions
document_sections.content: Following cataract surgery, TECNIS Puresee™ provided better intermediate and near vision than the enhanced monofocal comparator while preserving comparable distance vision and contrast sensitivity. The authors report substantial spectacle independence and patient satisfaction and regard the refractive EDOF lens as a promising presbyopia-correction option. They consider their real-world findings consistent with earlier preclinical simulations and the RCT. In their view, TECNIS Puresee™ may be valuable to cataract surgeons seeking strong distance and intermediate vision, functional near vision and acceptable photic phenomena.

document_sections.heading: Institutional Review Board Statement
document_sections.content: The Severance Hospital Institutional Review Board approved the study (IRB Approval No. 4-2024-0423; 30 May 2024). The investigators state that it followed the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent was waived because the study was retrospective, and the data were analyzed anonymously.
